lead.headline: A Thanksgiving storm cut power at WSSC Water's main plant, its third conservation alert of 2026
lead.dek: The Maryland utility asked 1.9 million customers to use water for essentials only for about 18 hours, and says $155 million of electrical upgrades at its Potomac plant are already identified.
body: WSSC Water asked its 1.9 million customers in Montgomery and Prince George's counties, Maryland, to use water for essential needs only from 2:30 p.m. on Thanksgiving Day, November 26, until 8:30 a.m. on Friday, November 27. A fallen tree brought down a power line feeding the Potomac Water Filtration Plant, which went offline briefly, according to chief operating officer Priscilla To, as reported by WUSA9. The utility said water stayed safe to drink and no boil advisory was needed.

The backup, the Patuxent Water Filtration Plant, was partway through a three week maintenance shutdown that WSSC usually schedules in the fall. Crews restarted it to add redundancy, and the utility said it would decide the following week whether to resume the work. The storm also caused intermittent power disruptions at both plants, FOX 5 DC reported, and by Friday morning WSSC said both were producing enough safe water to meet demand.

It was the third such request this year, after a six day alert in January tied to freezing weather and main breaks and a 32 hour restriction in late September when old electrical equipment failed at Potomac. WSSC has identified $155 million in electrical upgrades at Potomac, about $133 million of it priority work it wants to speed up, and is studying on-site power generation there. It is seeking outside and federal funding to keep bills affordable.

pipe.source: The Potomac River feeds the Potomac plant; the Patuxent reservoirs feed the second plant.
pipe.treat: A downed power line briefly took the Potomac plant offline while Patuxent was down for maintenance.
pipe.use: 1.9 million customers were asked to limit flushing, laundry and dishes to protect storage and fire flow.
pipe.reuse: Not a factor in this event; the issue was power supply to treatment.
pipe.discharge: Wastewater service was not reported as affected.

use.text: Check that backup plant maintenance is not scheduled into storm season.
Power resilience at plants is now a rate case line item.
Switchgear and on-site generation work at Potomac is coming.
Watch how WSSC funds $155 million of electrical upgrades.

briefs.headline: African Development Bank lends €71 million for a wastewater treatment and reuse complex in Monastir
briefs.text: The African Development Bank's board approved on November 25 a €71 million loan for a wastewater treatment and reuse complex in Monastir, Tunisia, announced November 27. The project costs €97.91 million in total; the Rome Process and Mattei Plan Financing Facility adds a €17 million loan and a €1.2 million grant, and the national sanitation office ONAS, which leads the work, puts in €8.71 million. The plant is meant to raise treatment capacity, supply treated water to farms and factories in a region with a large textile industry, and cut pollution into the Mediterranean.
briefs.why: Blended European and development bank money is becoming the standard way North African reuse projects get financed.

briefs.headline: Desalination contract awards are set to fall to 4.5 million m³ a day this year despite a record pipeline
briefs.text: About 4.1 million cubic meters a day of desalination capacity had been awarded in 2026 as of the IDRA Desalination and Reuse Handbook 2026-2027, released November 26, and the total is expected to reach about 4.5 million by year end, down from more than 6 million in 2025. Conflict has constrained Gulf activity since March, and large Gulf tenders that drew four to six bidders now typically draw one to three. Mega plant build prices have risen to about $1,000 per m³ a day of capacity from $700 before the pandemic, and no award in the past year beat Dubai's Hassyan benchmark tariff of $0.365 per m³. Morocco is now the second largest five year opportunity after Saudi Arabia.
briefs.why: Fewer bidders and higher build costs mean the delayed Gulf tenders, when they come, may price above recent benchmarks.

briefs.headline: ADB approves $468 million for irrigation and flash flood projects in Pakistan
briefs.text: The Asian Development Bank approved two concessional loans totaling $468 million for water and farming projects reaching about 728,000 people, The Nation reported November 28. A $208 million loan funds resilient irrigation and farm technology in the Nowshera, Swabi and Upper Chitral districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, with a role for women in water governance. A $260 million loan funds hill torrent management in Punjab: flash flood mitigation, floodwater harvesting, spate irrigation and aquifer recharge.
briefs.why: Capturing flash floods for irrigation and recharge is a growing share of development bank water lending in South Asia.

briefs.headline: A $150 million ADB loan will build water networks with smart meters in eight Bangladeshi towns
briefs.text: The Asian Development Bank approved a $150 million concessional loan for water supply and sanitation in eight fast growing Bangladeshi towns serving about 900,000 people, Xinhua reported November 27. The project covers about 1,790 kilometers of distribution pipe and 65,000 new or rehabilitated household connections with smart meters, plus household latrines and public sanitation run by women residents. The government adds $46 million, a separate $1 million package supports utility governance reform, and completion is expected in December 2032.
briefs.why: Metering every new connection from the start is how lenders now try to keep non-revenue water low in new systems.

briefs.headline: An Illinois bill would bar data centers from charging cooling systems with sole-source aquifer water
briefs.text: Illinois state Sen. Chapin Rose filed Senate Bill 4242, the Data Center Transparency and Aquifer Protection Act, The News-Gazette reported November 27. It would bar data centers from using water from the Mahomet Aquifer or any other sole-source aquifer to initially charge or recharge cooling systems, let the state shut down a data center on a community supply if falling groundwater threatens existing customers, and require water use reporting and impact reviews. It also requires public notice and a hearing before local governments negotiate with a proposed data center and limits nondisclosure agreements.
briefs.why: It follows bills filed in Texas this month; state rules on data center water are arriving before federal ones.

company.name: VA Tech Wabag
company.headline: Wabag's order book passed ₹20,000 crore, then Saudi Arabia pulled a big one
company.body: The Chennai based water treatment and desalination contractor reported first half revenue up 20% to about ₹1,887 crore and net profit up 29% to about ₹195 crore for the period to September 30, with net cash for a 15th straight quarter. Chairman and managing director Rajiv Mittal pointed to two large desalination orders, a seawater plant in Kuwait and a plant at Jamnagar in India. Management said revenue growth could reach the top of its 15% to 20% guidance. Nine days later the Saudi Water Authority cancelled the 300,000 cubic meter a day Yanbu award, and the company said it is seeking the reasons before deciding next steps.

leader.name: Yang Seung-jo
leader.role: Chief executive, Korea Water Resources Corporation (K-water)

figs.l: Daily supply planned for Honam fabs

leader.body: Yang has started his term at K-water's helm on the chip file. His first official field trip, on November 18, was to SK hynix's Yongin cluster to discuss timely supply and plans to localize ultrapure water production. On November 20 he inspected Juam and Dongbok dams, the main sources for the planned Honam semiconductor complex, where K-water plans to supply about 600,000 cubic meters a day and build 1.06 million of capacity to cover future demand and drought. Dongbok Dam is being raised 15 meters so it can send 300,000 cubic meters a day to the complex.

supplier.name: Kemira
supplier.headline: Kemira is buying its way into industrial water services while raw material costs squeeze margins
body: Kemira, the Helsinki based maker of coagulants, flocculants and other chemicals for water intensive industries, employs about 4,900 people. On October 23 it reported third quarter revenue of €709 million, up 3%, with flat organic growth and about €18 million added by acquisitions. Chief executive Antti Salminen kept full year guidance of €2.6 to €3.0 billion in revenue and €400 to €500 million in operative EBITDA.

Water Solutions, its largest segment, grew revenue 5% to €331 million, mainly through acquisitions, with a 19.7% operative EBITDA margin. Kemira closed the purchase of Nebraska based Water Engineering, an industrial water treatment services firm serving food and beverage, manufacturing and healthcare, in October 2025, then added ANMAC Water Treatment Service and Italy's REPUR, which provides activated carbon services, in the third quarter.

The pressure is on costs. Group operative EBITDA margin fell to 15.9% from 20.0% as variable costs rose €35 million against €11 million of price increases, and Kemira puts the gross 2026 cost impact of the Middle East conflict at about €100 million, roughly half of it mitigated. On November 23 it said it will invest in a venture fund to back startup innovation.
supplier.why: Activated carbon and service contracts put Kemira closer to the PFAS and industrial reuse spending wave. Watch whether price increases catch up with input costs in 2027.

innovation.name: University of Rochester
innovation.headline: A Rochester lab desalinates seawater without leaving brine behind
innovation.body: Most desalination plants send concentrated brine back to the sea. A team led by Chunlei Guo at the University of Rochester's Institute of Optics built a solar thermal system that uses no chemical additives and discharges no liquid brine, extracting nearly 100% of the dissolved salts in solid form. It tested real seawater from the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans and published the work in Light: Science & Applications. A related study recovered about half the lithium in salts left after desalination, using Great Salt Lake samples. The work is at laboratory stage, and the release gives no flow rate or cost figures.

investor.name: Emerald Technology Ventures
investor.headline: A Zurich venture firm that brought the water majors in as backers
investor.body: Founded in 2000, Emerald manages and advises over €1 billion from offices in Zurich, Toronto and Singapore. Its second water fund reached €100 million in March after Temasek and the Grundfos Foundation joined anchor investors Veralto and Ecolab, with SKion Water and Oxy Technology Ventures. The first water fund closed in 2020 at $100 million. It backs early to growth stage companies in treatment, reuse, monitoring and emerging contaminants, and lists exits to SUEZ, Xylem and BASF. Helge Daebel heads the water practice.

capital.intro: Private equity has executed 435 water deals across 25 countries since 2015 and more than doubled its holdings since 2019, according to Bluefield Research. Most of those assets are under three years old, which points to an exit wave.

firm.name: Sciens Water
firm.headline: Sciens Water builds platforms, from small utilities to century-old filter makers
firm.body: Sciens Water is the water arm of Sciens Capital Management, an alternative asset manager founded in 1994. Its first platform, Central States Water Resources of St. Louis, is a regulated utility that buys and rehabilitates small, struggling water and wastewater systems. The second, Veyra of Austin, formerly Integrated Water Services, sells decentralized treatment and added reverse osmosis through acquisitions this year. In November, through Fund II, it bought Roberts Filter Group, a Pennsylvania maker of gravity filters founded in 1889, to serve large utilities. John Rigas is chairman and CEO.

security.headline: The UN says the world has entered water bankruptcy
security.text: A UN University report in January argued that groundwater depletion, overallocation and pollution have pushed many basins past the point of recovery, and that "crisis" no longer describes it.

place.name: Basilica Cistern
place.headline: A sixth century reservoir held up by a forest of 336 columns
body: Built between 532 and 542 under the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian I, the Basilica Cistern, Yerebatan Sarnıcı in Turkish, was one of the city's major water stores, with an estimated capacity of about 100,000 tons. Its roof rests on 336 columns, each 9 meters tall.

Two carved Medusa heads, identified in 1986, serve as column bases, one upside down and one on its side. The cistern opened to visitors in 1987 after a major restoration, and reopened on July 22, 2022 after a second restoration that began in 2014.
place.visit: In Istanbul's historic peninsula; open as a museum. Check opening hours and tickets before you go.
place.why: Istanbul hosts the IWRA World Water Congress in October 2027, and this is the city's oldest lesson in storing water close to demand.
